'''''Xanthium strumarium''''' ('''rough cocklebur''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''Noogoora burr''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Noogoora burr (Xanthium occidentale) |url=https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/WeedImages/Details/320?NoWeeds=9 |website=NSW WeedWise|access-date=2024-04-08}}</ref> '''clotbur''', '''common cocklebur''', '''large cocklebur''', '''woolgarie bur''', '''Siberian cocklebur''') is a species of annual plants in the [[flowering plant]] family [[Asteraceae]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Everitt|first1=J.H.|last2=Lonard|first2=R.L.|last3=Little|first3=C.R.|title=Weeds in South Texas and Northern Mexico|year=2007|publisher=Texas Tech University Press|location=Lubbock|isbn=978-0-89672-614-7}}</ref> Some sources claim it originates in southern Europe and Asia, but has been extensively naturalized elsewhere.<ref name="260893-1"/><ref>{{cite web|title=''Xanthium strumarium''|work=Atlas of Florida Plants|publisher=Institute for Systematic Botany, University of South Florida|url= https://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=1348}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Xanthium strumarium L.|url= https://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=8367|id=Taxon Report 8367|publisher=Calflora}}</ref> Others, such as the Flora of China and Flora of North America, state it originates in the Americas but was an early introduction to Eurasia.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|220014370|Xanthium strumarium |family=Asteraceae |last=Strother |first=John L. |volume=21 |access-date=July 27, 2022}}</ref><ref name="FOC">{{eFloras|2|220014370|Xanthium strumarium |family=Asteraceae |last=Shi |first=Zhu |volume=20-21 |access-date=July 27, 2022}}</ref>

==Reproductive biology==
The species is monoecious, with the flowers borne in separate unisexual heads: staminate (male) heads situated above the pistillate (female) heads in the inflorescence.<ref>{{cite journal | last1= Weaver | first1= S.E. | last2=Lechowicz |first2=M.J. | title = The biology of Canadian weeds. 56. 'Xanthium strumarium' L. | year = 1983 |volume=63 |number=1 |doi=10.4141/cjps83-021 | journal = Canadian Journal of Plant Science | pages= 211–225 | bibcode= 1983CJPlS..63..211W }}
</ref> The pistillate heads consist of two pistillate flowers surrounded by a spiny [[Bract|involucre]]. Upon fruiting, these two flowers ripen into two brown to black achenes and they are completely enveloped by the involucre, which becomes a [[bur]]. The bur, being buoyant, easily disperses in the water for plants growing along waterways. However, the bur, with its hooked projections, is obviously adapted to dispersal via mammals by becoming entangled in their hair. Once dispersed and deposited on the ground, typically one of the seeds germinates and the plants grows out of the bur.

==Toxic or medicinal phytochemistry==
The plant may have some medicinal properties<ref>{{cite journal|author=Kamboj Anjoo |author2=Saluja Ajay Kumar |title=Phytopharmacological review of Xanthium strumarium L. (Cocklebur) |date=2010 |journal=International Journal of Green Pharmacy|volume=4|issue=3|pages=129–139|doi= 10.4103/0973-8258.69154 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and has been used in traditional medicine in [[South Asia]] and [[traditional Chinese medicine]]. In [[Telugu language|Telugu]], this plant is called Marula Matangi.

However, while small quantities of parts of the mature plants may be consumed, the seeds and seedlings should not be eaten in large quantities because they contain significant concentrations of the extremely toxic chemical [[carboxyatractyloside]]. The mature plant also contains at least four other toxins.<ref>{{Cite journal
 |vauthors=Islam MR, Uddin MZ, Rahman MS, Tutul E, Rahman MZ, Hassan MA, Faiz MA, Hossain M, Hussain M, Rashid MA
  | title = Ethnobotanical, phytochemical and toxicological studies of Xanthium strumarium L
 | journal = Bangladesh Medical Research Council Bulletin
 | volume = 35
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 84–90
 | date = Dec 2009
 | doi = 10.3329/bmrcb.v35i3.3658
 | pmid=20922910| doi-access = free
}}</ref>
*Animals have also been known to die after eating the plants.
*A patient consuming a traditional Chinese medicine containing cocklebur called ''Cang Er Zi Wan'' (苍耳子丸) developed muscle spasms.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | vauthors = West PL, Mckeown NJ, Hendrickson RG
 | title = Muscle spasm associated with therapeutic use of Cang Er Zi Wan.
 | journal = Clinical Toxicology
 | volume = 48
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 380–4
 | date = May 2010
 | doi = 10.3109/15563651003610161
 | pmid=20521353| s2cid = 25015169
 }}</ref>
* It was responsible for at least 19 deaths and 76 illnesses in [[Sylhet]] District, [[Bangladesh]], 2007. People ate large amounts of the plants, locally called ''ghagra shak'', because they were starving during a [[monsoon]] [[flood]] and no other plants were available. The symptoms included vomiting and altered mental states, followed by unconsciousness.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | vauthors = Gurley ES, Rahman M, Hossain MJ, Nahar N, Faiz MA, Islam N, Sultana R, Khatun S, Uddin MZ, Haider MS, Islam MS, Ahmed BN, Rahman MW, Mondal UK, Luby SP
